summary.text: For any sufficiently large prime \(p\), let \(j\) be minimal with \(2p\le \binom{j+1}{2}\); then \(2p\) is a composite factor of the product for block \(j\), while \(\binom{j+2}{2}<3p\) ensures that the next block contains no multiple of \(p\), so the former product cannot divide the latter. Choosing arbitrarily large primes makes the corresponding indices \(j+1\) unbounded, yielding infinitely many divisibility failures.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_m=\binom m2=\frac{m(m-1)}2.
\]
Thus the block used to define the sequence at index \(m\) is
\[
B_m=(C_m,C_{m+1}]\cap\mathbb N
   =\{C_m+1,C_m+2,\ldots,C_{m+1}\}.
\]
If \(Q_m\) denotes the set of composite integers in \(B_m\), then
\[
a(m)=\prod_{q\in Q_m}q,
\]
with the empty product understood to be \(1\). We will prove that the set
\[
\mathcal B=\{n>1:a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\}
\]
is unbounded, and hence infinite.

We use the elementary recurrence
\[
C_{m+1}=C_m+m.
\]
Consequently,
\[
C_{m+2}=C_m+2m+1.
\]
We will also need the following estimate: if \(m\ge 9\), then
\[
4m\le C_m.
\]
Indeed, \(m-1\ge 8\), so
\[
2C_m=m(m-1)\ge 8m,
\]
and division by \(2\) gives the claim.

Now let \(p\ge 23\) be prime. Since the numbers \(C_{r+1}\) tend to infinity, there is a least nonnegative integer \(j\) such that
\[
2p\le C_{j+1}.
\]
By minimality,
\[
C_j<2p. \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, \(j\ge 10\). To see this, if \(j<10\), then \(j+1\le 10\), and monotonicity of the binomial coefficients gives
\[
C_{j+1}\le C_{10}=\binom{10}{2}=45.
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge 23\) gives \(2p\ge 46\), contradicting \(2p\le C_{j+1}\).

We next establish the crucial upper bound
\[
C_{j+2}<3p. \tag{2}
\]
Since \(j\ge 10\), in particular \(j\ge 9\), and therefore
\[
4j\le C_j.
\]
Combining this with (1) yields
\[
4j<2p,
\]
so \(2j<p\). Since all quantities are integers, this implies
\[
2j+1\le p.
\]
Using the recurrence for \(C_m\), we now obtain
\[
C_{j+2}=C_j+2j+1<2p+p=3p,
\]
which proves (2).

By the definition of \(j\), we have
\[
C_j<2p\le C_{j+1}.
\]
Thus \(2p\) lies in the block \(B_j=(C_j,C_{j+1}]\). It is composite because both factors \(2\) and \(p\) are greater than \(1\). Hence \(2p\) is one of the factors occurring in the product \(a(j)\). It follows that
\[
p\mid a(j). \tag{3}
\]

We claim, in contrast, that
\[
p\nmid a(j+1). \tag{4}
\]
In fact, no integer at all in the next block
\[
B_{j+1}=(C_{j+1},C_{j+2}]
\]
is divisible by \(p\). Suppose for contradiction that some \(c\in B_{j+1}\) were divisible by \(p\). Write
\[
c=pk
\]
for a nonnegative integer \(k\). Because \(c\in B_{j+1}\),
\[
c>C_{j+1}\ge 2p.
\]
If \(k\le 2\), then \(c=pk\le 2p\), a contradiction. Therefore \(k\ge 3\), and hence
\[
c=pk\ge 3p.
\]
But the other endpoint inequality for the block, together with (2), gives
\[
c\le C_{j+2}<3p,
\]
another contradiction. This proves that no element of \(B_{j+1}\), and therefore no composite element of that block, is divisible by \(p\).

Since \(p\) is prime, if it divides a finite product then it divides at least one factor: this follows by repeatedly applying Euclid's lemma, which says that a prime dividing a product of two integers divides one of them. As none of the factors in \(a(j+1)\) is divisible by \(p\), their product is not divisible by \(p\). The same conclusion also holds if there are no composite factors, since then the product is \(1\). Thus (4) follows.

Equations (3) and (4) show that
\[
a(j)\nmid a(j+1).
\]
Indeed, if \(a(j)\mid a(j+1)\), then the divisibility \(p\mid a(j)\) would imply \(p\mid a(j+1)\), contrary to (4). Set
\[
n=j+1.
\]
Because \(j\ge 10\), certainly \(n>1\), and we have proved
\[
a(n-1)\nmid a(n). \tag{5}
\]
The construction also retains the useful size bound
\[
2p\le C_{j+1}=C_n. \tag{6}
\]

It remains to show that indices obtained this way are unbounded. Let \(N\) be any nonnegative integer. Choose a prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
p\ge \max\{23,C_{N+1}+1\}.
\]
Such a prime exists because primes are arbitrarily large. For completeness, this standard fact follows by considering, for any prescribed bound \(M\), a prime divisor of \(M!+1\): that prime cannot be at most \(M\), since every prime at most \(M\) divides \(M!\) and therefore cannot also divide \(M!+1\).

Apply the preceding construction to this prime \(p\), producing an index \(n=j+1\) satisfying (5) and (6). The choice of \(p\) gives
\[
2p>C_{N+1},
\]
and hence, by (6),
\[
C_n\ge 2p>C_{N+1}. \tag{7}
\]
If \(n\le N\), monotonicity of \(C_m=\binom m2\) would give
\[
C_n\le C_N\le C_{N+1},
\]
contradicting (7). Therefore \(n>N\).

We have consequently shown that for every \(N\) there exists \(n>N\) such that \(n>1\) and
\[
a(n-1)\nmid a(n).
\]
Thus \(\mathcal B\) is unbounded. Every finite set of natural numbers is bounded, so \(\mathcal B\) is infinite. Hence it is false that there are only finitely many integers \(n>1\) for which \(a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\).
